Path of a ray through a triangular prism; angle of prism A = r₁ + r₂

History: corpuscular model (Newton) vs wave model (Huygens)
Young's interference experiment and Maxwell's EM theory established wave nature
Ray optics as a limit of wave optics when wavelength is small compared with obstacles
Wavefront: surface of constant phase; spherical, cylindrical and plane wavefronts
Rays are normal to wavefronts; energy travels perpendicular to the wavefront
Huygens principle: every point of a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets; new wavefront is their forward envelope
Absence of backwave explained

sections.name: 10.3 Refraction and Reflection of Plane Waves using Huygens Principle

concepts.text: 10.3.1 Refraction of a plane wave: derivation of Snell's law sin i/sin r = v₁/v₂ = n₂/n₁

sections.name: 10.4 Coherent and Incoherent Addition of Waves

concepts.text: Coherent sources: constant phase difference; incoherent sources: phase difference varies randomly
Resultant intensity I = 4I₀ cos²(φ/2) for two coherent waves of equal intensity
Constructive interference for path difference nλ, destructive for (n + ½)λ

Young's double-slit setup: path difference ≈ xd/D at a point on the screen
Positions of bright fringes x = nλD/d and dark fringes x = (n + ½)λD/d (final expressions)

Energy is redistributed in interference, not destroyed

Comparison of interference and diffraction patterns (intensity, fringe widths)

chapters.title: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

concepts.text: Discovery of the electron via cathode rays (J.J. Thomson); e/m measurement and Millikan's oil drop charge

Free electrons in metals cannot leave the surface without extra energy
Work function φ₀: minimum energy needed to free an electron; measured in eV; table of work functions
Methods of emission: thermionic, field (cold cathode) and photoelectric emission
11.3.1 Hertz's observations: UV light enhanced sparks across a gap
11.3.2 Hallwachs' and Lenard's observations: UV light on zinc plate causes emission of electrons
Threshold frequency: no emission below a minimum frequency regardless of intensity
Photosensitive substances: alkali metals respond to visible light; zinc, cadmium need UV
Setup: evacuated tube with emitter (cathode) and collector (anode), variable potential and monochromatic source
11.4.1 Effect of intensity: photocurrent proportional to intensity for frequency above threshold
11.4.2 Effect of potential: photocurrent saturates; stopping potential V₀ reduces current to zero
Stopping potential is independent of intensity; eV₀ = Kmax
11.4.3 Effect of frequency: stopping potential increases linearly with frequency; graph of V₀ versus ν
Threshold frequency from the graph; slope same for all metals
Photoelectric emission is instantaneous (no time lag)

sections.name: 11.5 Photoelectric Effect and Wave Theory of Light

concepts.text: Wave theory predicts Kmax should depend on intensity - contradicted
Wave theory cannot explain threshold frequency or instantaneous emission

sections.name: 11.6 Einstein's Photoelectric Equation: Energy Quantum of Radiation

concepts.text: Radiation consists of quanta of energy hν; one photon ejects one electron
Einstein's equation Kmax = hν - φ₀ = eV₀
Threshold frequency ν₀ = φ₀/h and threshold wavelength
Explanation of all observations; Millikan's verification and value of h from slope h/e
Worked example type: maximum kinetic energy and stopping potential for given wavelength and work function
Worked example type: work function and threshold frequency from stopping potential data

sections.name: 11.7 Particle Nature of Light: The Photon

concepts.text: Photon properties: energy E = hν, momentum p = hν/c, speed c, zero rest mass
Intensity relates to number of photons, not photon energy
Photons are electrically neutral, not deflected by fields; number may change but energy and momentum conserved in collisions
Worked example type: number of photons emitted per second by a source of given power and wavelength
Worked example type: momentum and energy of a photon of given wavelength
de Broglie hypothesis: moving particles have wavelength λ = h/p = h/mv
Wavelength is negligible for macroscopic bodies, significant for electrons

Wave-particle duality of matter and radiation; electron microscope uses matter waves

Thomson's plum pudding model and its failure

sections.name: 12.2 Alpha-particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of Atom

concepts.text: Geiger-Marsden experiment: alpha particles on thin gold foil; detector with ZnS screen
Observations: most pass undeflected, few deflected through large angles, very few retraced
Conclusion: positive charge and most mass concentrated in a tiny nucleus
12.2.1 Alpha-particle trajectory depends on impact parameter; small b gives large scattering
Distance of closest approach from energy conservation (estimate of nuclear size)
Worked example type: distance of closest approach of alpha particle to gold nucleus
12.2.2 Electron orbits: centripetal force from Coulomb attraction; energy E = -e²/(8πε₀r)
Total energy negative means electron is bound to nucleus
Limitations of Rutherford model: accelerated electron should radiate and spiral into nucleus; cannot explain line spectra
Each element emits a characteristic emission line spectrum when excited
Absorption spectrum: dark lines at same wavelengths as emission lines
Spectra act as fingerprints for identifying elements

sections.name: 12.4 Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom

concepts.text: Postulate 1: electrons move in certain stable orbits without radiating (stationary states)
Postulate 2: angular momentum quantised L = nh/2π
Postulate 3: transition between orbits emits/absorbs a photon hν = Ei - Ef
Radius of nth orbit rn = n²h²ε₀/(πme²) ∝ n²; Bohr radius a₀ ≈ 0.53 Å (expression)
Speed of electron in nth orbit vn ∝ 1/n

Ionisation energy (13.6 eV) and excitation energy; continuous energy for unbound electron
Worked example type: energy, radius or speed for a given orbit; energy to ionise from excited state
Franck-Hertz experiment as evidence for discrete levels (noted)

sections.name: 12.5 The Line Spectra of the Hydrogen Atom

concepts.text: Line spectra explained by transitions between energy levels (qualitative)
Frequency of emitted photon ν = (13.6 eV/h)(1/nf² - 1/ni²); Rydberg constant
Emission and absorption lines correspond to same level differences
Worked example type: wavelength of photon emitted in a transition between given levels

sections.name: 12.6 de Broglie's Explanation of Bohr's Second Postulate of Quantisation

concepts.text: Electron in orbit as a standing matter wave; circumference equals whole number of wavelengths 2πr = nλ
Using λ = h/mv gives mvr = nh/2π, Bohr's quantisation condition
Limitations of Bohr model: works for hydrogen-like atoms only, no explanation of relative intensities
Exercise type: energy level diagram transitions, number of spectral lines, ratio of radii/energies

sections.name: 13.2 Atomic Masses and Composition of Nucleus

concepts.text: Atomic mass unit 1 u = 1/12 mass of carbon-12 atom = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg
Mass spectrometer measures atomic masses; isotopes explain non-integral atomic masses (chlorine)
Proton as hydrogen nucleus; neutron discovered by Chadwick (1932) from beryllium bombarded by alpha particles
Nucleus composition: Z protons, N neutrons, mass number A = Z + N; notation for nuclides
Isotopes (same Z), isobars (same A), isotones (same N) with examples

Short-range force; strongly attractive at a few fm, repulsive below about 0.8 fm
Charge independence: n-n, n-p, p-p forces nearly equal

Energy released by moving to nuclei with higher binding energy per nucleon
Comparison of energy released per reaction in chemical vs nuclear processes

Current due to motion of both electrons and holes (I = Ie + Ih)

p-type: trivalent acceptor (In, B, Al) creates holes; holes majority carriers
